THE CONTRACTOR SHALL MAINTAIN AN ACCURATE RECORD OF THE EXCAVATED MATERIAL INCLUDING NATURE OF SOIL AT FORMATION LEVEL AND GROUND WATER. Statement of Problem Urban infrastructures are becoming more complex last century. The importance of pipe detecting and the value of its application. Before excavation for maintenance of underground piping, it is necessary to understand the various site problems on topography and surface materials (e.g. position (depth and displacement) and size of other piping, as well as manholes); In order to prevent third party companies from possible damages to infrastructural equipments and people, severe damage will be generated from mistaken excavation of other piping. The severity might even affect the corporate image and living resources such as electricity, telecommunication and hydrology. Detection of underground pipeline and cable locations is very important, in addition, locations and positions of infrastructural elements with respect to each other must be known for the new infrastructural projects and for the process of operation and replacement of current infrastructure. 1.1. Introduction Developing Technologies are rapidly, so there are a lot of devices for the detection of pipeline and cable locations. These devices are working with two methods in general. One of them is electromagnetic detection method with electromagnetic induction, and the other is GPR (Ground Penetrating Radar) method working with the principle of determining the underground structure and underground holes. Especially with the new instruments and computer algorithms developed in the last years, the locations of infrastructural elements with respect to each other are determined more accurately. Ground penetrating radar (GPR) is a geophysical method that uses radar pulses to image the subsurface. This non-destructive method uses electromagnetic (EM) radiation in the microwave band (UHF/VHF frequencies) of the radio spectrum, and detects the reflected signals from subsurface structures. One of the most useful applications of GPR in urban infrastructural engineering is mapping and detection of buried pipes. This unique application becomes imperative due to the ever-growing urbanization in both developed and developing nations with its attendant demand for buried utilities. The construction, development and management of subsurface infrastructures has become a very viable business that attracts the attention of scientists and engineers over the past few years. Various utilities such as telecommunication and electric power cables, water and gas supply cables etc. are delivered through underground pipes of various sized buried at different depths. PIPE DIAMETER LESS THAN 300MM ARE HDPE PIPES (PN16) WITH SDR -11 PE-100 AND DIAMETER EQUAL TO AND GREATER THAN Ø300 DUCTILE IRON PIPES CLASS C AND OPERATING PRESSURE 24 BAR SHALL BE USED FOR WHOLE POTABLE & FIRE WATER SYSTEM. 3. GATE VALVES SHALL BE DIRECT BURIED WITH SURFACE BOXES FOR PIPE DIA LESS THAN Ø300 WHILE FOR PIPE DIAMETER EQUAL TO AND LARGER THAN Ø300 SHOULD BE IN CONCRETE CHAMBERS. BUTTERFLY VALVES SHALL BE INSTALLED INSIDE CONCRETE CHAMBERS FOR PIPE DIA EQUAL TO AND MORE THAN Ø300. 4. POTABLE & FIRE WATER LINE SHALL BE INSTALLED WITH A SOIL COVER DEPTH OF 1.2M UNDER MAJOR ROADS AND 1.0M UNDER LOCAL ROADS. 5. A HORIZONTAL SEPARATION OF 3 METERS AND A VERTICAL SEPARATION OF 0.50 METER SHALL BE MAINTAINED BETWEEN POTABLE WATER AND SEWER LINES WITH THE SEWER LINE BELOW THE WATER LINE. A HORIZONTAL SEPARATION OF MINIMUM 3.00 METERS SHALL BE MAINTAINED WHERE A MINIMUM OF 0.50 METER VERTICAL SEPARATION CANNOT BE ACHIEVED. AT CROSS OVERS, WHERE THE VERTICAL SEPARATION CANNOT BE MAINTAINED WITH WATER LINE, THE SEWER LINE SHALL BE ENCASED IN CONCRETE FOR A MINIMUM LENGTH OF 3.00 METERS ON EACH SIDE OF THE WATER LINE. 6. CONCRETE THRUST BLOCKS SHALL BE PROVIDED AT ALL PIPE BENDS, TEES, REDUCERS AND INCASE OF CHANGE IN DIRECTION BOTH HORIZONTAL AND VERTICAL FOR DUCTILE IRON PIPES. FOR HDPE COMPLY WITH SUPPLIER RECOMMENDATIONS, THRUST BLOCK WILL NOT BE REQUIRED FOR HDPE PIPE IF FUSION WELDED. 7. PIPES HAVING COVER LESS THAN 1.0M SHALL BE ENCASED IN PLAIN CONCRETE. 8. ALL SERVICE CONNECTION PIPES SHALL BE INSTALLED AT DEPTH 0.80 TO 1.0 METER FROM FINISHED GRADE LEVEL. 9. excerpt: Document history and status Distribution of copies Executive summary The attached details a number of obstacles following the planned clearance of the SEC site by the end of July 2025. The most concern lies in the connection of utilities which has not been factored into the SEC planned clearance pre-dominantly the reservoir overflow tank which cannot be moved and impedes the storm water connection as per below. The NGL (Natural Ground Level) has been built up with unscreened fill which need to removed to a Municipality dump as part of the works together with a number of other obstacles outlined within this report. Introduction The Contractor has been instructed by the Client to carry out the Gateway-1 Infrastructure work. Gateway-1 is located at the northern side of the Northern Ring Road as indicated in the below pictures. The Scope of the work related to the Infra-1 contractor is indicated in the below snip The area was previously occupied by Saudi Electric Company (SEC) as a laydown area for the construction of the HV substations and network. Following the instruction to AICC to carry out the infrastructure work at Gatweway-1, a site visit was carried out to assess the existing conditions of the site and to enable the site handover from SEC to Infra-1. Site Obstacles Several obstacles within the Right-of-Way (ROW) of the infra-1 have been identified as indicated in the below snip. The details of the above-mentioned obstacles are listed in the below table: Site Topography The site topography has been artificially raised by approximately 1 to 4 meters using unconsolidated fill materials and construction debris (refer to the images below). These materials must be excavated and removed to restore the site to its original natural ground level (NGL) before commencing earthwork activities. At present, the exact volume of these materials cannot be accurately determined due to the lack of historical elevation data. However, a preliminary estimate suggests that the volume of unconsolidated material is approximately 30,000 cubic meters. THE SURVEY COORDINATE SYSTEM IS WGS84 - UTM 38 N AND LOCAL VERTICAL DATUM. 4. ALL DIMENSIONS SHALL BE VERIFIED ON SITE BEFORE PROCEEDING WITH THE WORK. 5. ALL DIMENSIONS SHOWN ON STANDARD DETAIL DRAWINGS ARE IN MILLIMETERS UNLESS OTHERWISE INDICATED. 6. THE CONTRACTOR HAS TO TAKE ALL NECESSARY PRECAUTIONS AND MEASURES TO DEAL WITH GROUNDWATER AND SURFACE WATER DURING CONSTRUCTION IN CASE WATER TABLE IS ENCOUNTERED. 7. THE CONTRACTOR SHALL VERIFY GROUND LEVELS BEFORE COMMENCEMENT OF WORK. 8. VORTEX MANHOLES AND OIL INTERCEPTORS ARE PROPRIETARY ITEMS AND IT SHALL BE THE CONTRACTOR'S RESPONSIBILITY TO DESIGN AND CONSTRUCT AS PER MANUFACTURER'S STANDARDS AND RECOMMENDATIONS AND AS APPROVED BY THE EMPLOYER'S REPRESENTATIVE. 9. ANY DEVIATIONS FROM THE ALLOCATED CORRIDORS SHALL BE AGREED WITH THE EMPLOYER'S REPRESENTATIVE PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION COMMENCEMENT. 10. COVER LEVEL OF MANHOLES/CHAMBERS SHOULD MATCH WITH SURROUNDING BITUMINOUS /PAVED AREAS. 11. ALL CONCRETE SHALL BE CLASS 'A' UNLESS OTHERWISE INDICATED. SULFATE RESISTING PORTLAND CEMENT (TYPE V) COMPLYING WITH BS 4027 SHALL BE USED IN ALL CONCRETE MIXES. 12. STEEL REINFORCEMENT SHALL BE GRADE 460 (BS 4449) STEEL BARS OR AS SPECIFIED. 13. ALL REINFORCEMENT IN MANHOLES/CHAMBERS SHALL BE EPOXY COATED AS SPECIFIED. 14. MINIMUM COVER TO REINFORCEMENT SHALL BE 50mm, UNLESS SPECIFIED OTHERWISE . 15. EXTERNAL CONCRETE SURFACES BELOW GROUND SHALL BE PROTECTED WITH BITUMINOUS WATERPROOF MEMBRANE 2.20mm AND PROTECTION BOARD 6.0mm AS SPECIFIED. 16. GRANOLITHIC CONCRETE SHALL BE FORMED IN ALL MANHOLE CHANNELS TO PROVIDE A SMOOTH TRANSITION OF SIZE AND GRADIENT FROM THE INLET(S) TO THE OUTLET STORM INVERTS. 17. ALL MANHOLES TO HAVE 3 COATS OF EPOXY PAINT PROTECTION LINING TO ALL EXPOSED INTERNAL CONCRETE SURFACES. 18. INTERNAL CEMENT MORTAR JOINTS OF STORM MANHOLE EXTENSION RINGS SHALL BE RAKED OUT AND ALL EXPOSED FACES SHALL BE LAMINATED WITH EPOXY PAINT. 19. ALL PIPES CONNECTED TO THE MANHOLES ARE TO BE PROVIDED WITH ADEQUATE PUDDLE FLANGES AS REQUIRED. 20. ALL STORM MANHOLES SHALL BE FITTED WITH HEAVY DUTY D400 DI COVERS TO BS EN 124. 21. GRANULAR BED AND SURROUND TO PIPES SHALL BE ENCLOSED IN GEOTEXTILE AS SPECIFIED FOR ALL PIPES. 22. ANY PIPELINE BELOW GROUND LEVEL ENTERING OR PROTRUDING FROM ANY STRUCTURE SHALL BE FITTED WITH TWO FLEXIBLE JOINTS ADJACENT TO THE STRUCTURE AS SPECIFIED UNLESS INDICATED OTHERWISE. 23. CONCRETE SURROUND SHALL BE PROVIDED TO STORMWATER PIPES WHERE THE COVER IS LESS THAN 1.2 METERS. 24. THE OIL INTERCEPTORS SHOWN IN THE DRAWINGS ARE OPTIONAL AND WILL BE USED IN CASE THERE IS NO OIL INTERCEPTOR LOCATED BEFORE THE POND IN THE WADI AREA. 25. INLET TYPE (EITHER CATCH BASIN OR KERB INLET) ARE INDICATIVE FOLLOWING THE DESIGN AND CORRIDORS. IN CASE CONTRACTOR FOUND ON SITE THAT TYPE OF INLET NEEDS TO BE CHANGED FOLLOWING THE ROAD AND SITE CONDITIONS , HE CAN PROCEED ACCORDINGLY. 26. excerpt: Case Report Review of AMCO (Asset Management Company) Interfaces with Infrastructure team and Inherent delays Role Stakeholder Authority within Diriyah with specific oversight on Asset Management AMCO specifically reviewing all elements of the project that will be managed by them following Handover. Traffic Management Traffic Lighting Streetlighting ICT / Security Structure Breakdown in Terms of Infra Package 1 – AMCO Review Team Pedestrian underpasses – shared with AMCO on 15th Jan 2025 Traffic Management – Shared with AMCO on 21st Feb 2025 ICT/Security – shared with AMCO on 6th Feb 2025 Drafted By Clive Walsh Assoc Project Director 26th March 2025 Package Submission Review Package 1 Submission Description Underpass Structure (BVD and UPASS 2) Submission Date 15.01.25 Issue Type E-mail Days Overdue (allowing 14 days) 60 days Package 2 Submission Description Traffic Management Submission Date 21.02.25 Days Overdue (allowing 14 days) 19 days Package 3 Submission Description ICT/Security Submission Date 06.02.25 Days Overdue (allowing 14 days) 34 days Current Permit Flow Assessment Marked Red below – Areas where the PMC Stakeholder management team should be monitoring and requesting escalation but not happening Permit Flow-Diagram Review Key Observations and Findings AMCO have raised queries on the packages which have not been effectively communicated. This needs more investigation noting comments from Traffic Management package were received on 6th February 2025 and returned on 18th March 2025 (32 days to respond from DC team) and there is no other evidence of comments issued on the other packages. We note in addition that there is no set defined ruling for receipt of submissions with some using ACX ie. ICT and others standard mail with external zip files. (Appendix 1.0) AMCO requested a form to be completed referencing “AM Purpose of Request” The form returned was– noting Land Handover form issued and email (Appendix 2) – noting this is the request form but really does not suit the purpose of what’s required 3.0 No direct authorized person from Infrastructure DG2 Package 1 team following up is evident due to the passage of time without any visibility. Nobody owns the issue. Falling between two stools ; Nawar and Joao both poorly failing to address the key issues and no record of sufficient escalation controls evident. 4.0 Unclear Submissions referencing correspondence below leads to delays in Package Understanding Lots of examples of unclear direction and confusion on both sides of the Issuing and Receiving scale. Clear Roles and Responsibilities needed on both sides. 5.0 Consistent and Poor reporting by PMC Stakeholder management team. Noticing there is only a reporting functionality with Engr Anas (AECOM) with the weekly stakeholder meeting and reporting but no visible escalation and monitoring of consistent delays. This could be very well as a result of continuous delays in absolutely everything and now the team is tired to expedite anything and changes are recommended. 6.0 On both visits to AMCO on 25th and 26th March we found both key persons references marked “*” were working from home and unavailable. Rayan Bakhit Commercial Asst Manager*Abdul Rouf Bandith Assoc Design Direction *Abdul Haman Al Amri Design Director Key

excerpt: for Detection and Verification of Existing Underground Utilities The Purpose of this is to detection and verification of the underground utilitiesprior to commencement of any excavation works to ensure safety of the project operatives, personnel and the public; to avoid damages to buried utilities and assets. The process described in this can be summarized in the following : : Desktop utility record search includes the process of deification of the existing utilities within the survey area or the scope of work limits through the collation and analysis of existing as-built records. This should be carried out through the following process: Identify utility owners within the limit of works or survey area using the following source of information: Utility as-built drawings provided by the Client, PMC or the Engineer. BALADY Coordination certificate obtained by the Contractor. Refer to Appendix-1 for a sample of the coordination certificate. Note: Potential utility owners include SEC, NWC, Traffic police, Riyadh Municipality, DGCL AMCO, SWC, MODA, STC, Mobily, MEWA, etc. Upon identification of the affected utility owners, the Contractor will approach the identified utility owners to solicit up-to-date information and as-built drawings regarding the existing utilities. Deliverable of this step: The Contractor should collate the obtained as-built information and produce combined utility as-built records. The mentioned records to be composed of colored utility lines imposed on aerial images. Utility lines should indicate (as applicable) utility owner, type of utility, size, and depth (e.g. NWC; PW line, DI 300 mm, 1.5 m depth). Above records should be reviewed and approved by the CSC. Site reconnaissance shall compromise of a joint site visit by the Contractor and the CSC to validate the existing utility records obtained from step-1 and document the following: The presence of utility related surface features including manholes, inspection chambers, utility markers, feeder pillars, street lighting, traces of excavated trenches on paved roads, etc. Measurements between known surface features on the ground compared with those indicated in the utility records. Assessment of any conflicts between obtained utility records and actual site conditions. Deliverables of this step should include mark-up of the utility records along with supporting photographs. Detection: Detection involves the use of geophysical techniques to detect and locate the underground utilities within the survey area. Two techniques are generally applied to locate buried utilities: EML, Electro Magnetic Locating: Detection of buried utilities via a hand-held receiver using electromagnetic and radio frequency signals that are present in metallic utilities because of current flow or re-transmitted low frequency radio signals. GPR, Ground Penetrating Radar: The use of radar waves from a surface transmitter that can penetrate through ground materials and are reflected back to the instrument by a change of ground materials or other buried objects. The process of scanning utilities shall be as outlined below: Scanning device: The Contractor shall Submit technical data sheet, user manual, and calibration certificate for the CSC review / information. The Contractor to provide details of the device operator. Evidence of training provided either by the device manufacturer or amanufacturers’ s endorsed trainer has to be submitted to the CSC. BUTTERFLY VALVES SHALL BE INSTALLED INSIDE CONCRETE CHAMBERS FOR PIPE DIA EQUAL TO AND MORE THAN Ø300. 4) IRRIGATION LINE SHALL BE INSTALLED WITH A SOIL COVER DEPTH OF 1.2m UNDER MAJOR ROADS AND 1.0m UNDER LOCAL ROADS. 5) THRUST BLOCK FOR HDPE PIPE SHALL COMPLY WITH SUPPLIER RECOMMENDATIONS, THRUST BLOCK WILL NOT BE REQUIRED FOR HDPE PIPE IF FUSION WELDED. CONCRETE THRUST BLOCKS SHALL BE PROVIDED FOR ALL OTHER PIPES AT ALL PIPE BENDS, TEES, REDUCERS AND INCASE OF CHANGE IN DIRECTION BOTH HORIZONTAL AND VERTICAL FOR DUCTILE IRON PIPES. 6) PIPES HAVING COVER LESS THAN 1.0m SHALL BE ENCASED IN PLAIN CONCRETE. 7) PRESSURE CAN BE REDUCED TO DESIRED LEVEL USING PRV AT PLOT CONNECTION (MAXIMUM 5 BAR) AND AT SOLENOID VALVE(MAXIMUM 7BAR). ALL PRV INSTALLATION SHALL FOLLOW THE ARRANGEMENT AS SHOWN IN STANDARD DETAILS DRAWING. 8) FOR EXACT LOCATION OF IRRIGAITON PIPE LINE REFER TO TYPICAL UTILITIES COORDINATION CROSS SECTIONS DRAWINGS. 9) INSTALL AIR / VACUUM RELIEF VALVES AT IRRIGATION MAIN LINE TERMINATION POINTS, OR TO HIGHEST POINTS AND FINAL LOCATION TO BE ADJUSTED SITE. 10) ALL PIPE DIAMETERS ARE NOMINAL PIPE SIZES, FOR HDPE, IT IS OUTSIDE AND FOR GRP, IT IS INSIDE. 11) CONTRACTOR SHALL COORDINATE THE LOCAL AUTHORITIES / MUNICIPALITIES TO OBTAIN THE CONSTRUCTION APPROVAL BEFORE CONSTRUCTION. 12) ALL EXISITNG UTILITIES SYSTEMS SHALL BE KEPT IN OPERATION UNTIL THE NEW SYSTEM IS PUT IN TO OPERATION, AND IN FULL COORDINAITON WITH CONCERNED AUTHORITIES. 13) THE IRRIGATION SYSTEM IS DISPLAYED DIAGRAMMATIC, AND THE CONTRACTOR MAY BE REQUIRED TO MAKE ADJUSTMENTS IN THE FIELD AT THE TIME OF INSTALLATION TO AVOID EXISTING OR PLANNED UTILITIES. THE CONTRACTOR, HOWEVER, IS ADVISED TO FOLLOW THE LAYOUT AS SHOWN ON THE PLAN AS MUCH AS POSSIBLE 14) INCASE OF CONFLICT OR DISCREPANCY BETWEEN THE INFORMATION SHOWN AND ACTUAL CONDITION ON SITE, CONTRACTOR SHALL PREPARE SHOP DRAWING AND SUBMIT TO THE ENGINEER FOR APPROVAL PRIOR TO COMMENCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION. 15) FOR INTERFACE CONNECTION, CONTRACTOR SHALL BE RESPONSIBLE TO LOCATE THE EXISTING SOURCE (INTERFACE POINT) FOR THE PROJECT AREA AND MAKE CONNECTION WITH IRRIGATION MAIN SUPPLY SYSTEM. 16) THE CONTRACTOR SHALL COORDINATE WITH ALL RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITIES AND MINISTRIES REGARDING DATA OR LOCATION OF ALL EXISITNG UTILITIES AND REPORT TO THE ENGINEER. 17) THE CONTRACTOR WILL BE RESPONSIBLE FOR THE DISCONNECTION AND RECONNECTION OF THE EXISTING SERVICES TO THE NETWORK. 18) CONTRACTOR IS RESPONSIBLE TO VARIFY THE GROUND LEVELS. The site was divided into three main areas (see layout): 1- Media-1a 2- Boulevard North-west and Boulevard South- west. 3- Northern-west and Northen-Central. 1- Media-1a 1.1 Road R_00_11 from Chainage 0+500 to 0+900 Trench Depth: Varies from 3 m to 6 m. Trench gets deeper as it goes downstream to the outfall point near Wadi Finger-1 Ground conditions: Granular backfill at the top 1 to 2 m. Hard limestone at the underneath layers. excerpt: Diriyah Gate II Development 48 4.5 Pre-Construction Survey Prior to the commencement of construction and demolition activities, a pre-construction survey must be undertaken to identify all environmental aspects such as the following (but not limited to): ▪ Air Quality: - Visual and PM10 monitoring at Project boundary points located near identified SRs; ▪ Noise and Vibration Levels: - Baseline conditions should be monitored one month before commencement of construction and demolition activities; ▪ Soil contamination. A visual or olfactory inspection should be undertaken for the following: - Inspection for any contamination and spillages; - Identification of land uses and activities with potential sources of contamination; - Discoloured soil and/or fibrous texture to the soil (e.g., asbestos). Odour can also indicate contamination with the release of noxious fumes; - Foreign objects present; - Previous soil workings; - Waste pits; ▪ Water and wastewater: - If dewatering is required, baseline groundwater monitoring (including groundwater levels and quality) shall be undertaken; ▪ Ecology: - A terrestrial ecology survey will be undertaken in the form of a site walkover around the Project area, work site areas, access roads and buildings; - Pre-construction monitoring should be undertaken to locate potential ecological assets that may require relocation / protection (e.g., native trees, lizard burrows, nesting birds and roosting bats); ▪ Archaeology / Cultural Heritage: - Surveys carried out by professional archaeologists; - Drone survey; - Demarcation of areas with potential archaeological significance; ▪ Traffic and Transport; - Baseline traffic and routes assessment is recommended for planning of routes; and, - Noise and vibration monitoring. Photographic evidence of baseline conditions shall form part of the pre-construction survey. 4.6 Environmental and Sustainability Monitoring and Reporting MOSTADAM for Communities and LEED for Cities are the preferred certification schemes to be pursued and will be adopted at various target levels and in various districts of DG II. THE SURVEY COORDINATE SYSTEM IS WGS84 - UTM 38 N AND LOCAL VERTICAL DATUM. 4. ALL DIMENSIONS SHALL BE VERIFIED ON SITE BEFORE PROCEEDING WITH THE WORK. 5. ALL DIMENSIONS SHOWN ON STANDARD DETAIL DRAWINGS ARE IN MILLIMETERS UNLESS OTHERWISE INDICATED. 6. THE CONTRACTOR HAS TO TAKE ALL NECESSARY PRECAUTIONS AND MEASURES TO DEAL WITH GROUNDWATER AND SURFACE WATER DURING CONSTRUCTION IN CASE WATER TABLE IS ENCOUNTERED. 7. THE CONTRACTOR SHALL VERIFY GROUND LEVELS BEFORE COMMENCEMENT OF WORK. 8. OIL INTERCEPTOR ARE PROPRIETARY ITEMS AND IT SHALL BE THE CONTRACTOR'S RESPONSIBILITY TO DESIGN AND CONSTRUCT AS PER MANUFACTURER'S STANDARDS AND RECOMMENDATIONS AND AS APPROVED BY THE EMPLOYER'S REPRESENTATIVE. 9. ANY DEVIATIONS FROM THE ALLOCATED CORRIDORS SHALL BE AGREED WITH THE EMPLOYER'S REPRESENTATIVE PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION COMMENCEMENT. 10. COVER LEVEL OF MANHOLES/CHAMBERS SHOULD MATCH WITH SURROUNDING BITUMINOUS /PAVED AREAS. 11. ALL CONCRETE SHALL BE CLASS 'A' UNLESS OTHERWISE INDICATED. SULFATE RESISTING PORTLAND CEMENT (TYPE V) COMPLYING WITH BS 4027 SHALL BE USED IN ALL CONCRETE MIXES. 12. STEEL REINFORCEMENT SHALL BE GRADE 460 (BS 4449) STEEL BARS OR AS SPECIFIED. 13. ALL REINFORCEMENT IN MANHOLES/CHAMBERS SHALL BE EPOXY COATED AS SPECIFIED. 14. MINIMUM COVER TO REINFORCEMENT SHALL BE 50mm, UNLESS SPECIFIED OTHERWISE . 15. EXTERNAL CONCRETE SURFACES BELOW GROUND SHALL BE PROTECTED WITH BITUMINOUS WATERPROOF MEMBRANE 2.20mm AND PROTECTION BOARD 6.0mm AS SPECIFIED. 16. GRANOLITHIC CONCRETE SHALL BE FORMED IN ALL MANHOLE CHANNELS TO PROVIDE A SMOOTH TRANSITION OF SIZE AND GRADIENT FROM THE INLET(S) TO THE OUTLET STORM INVERTS. 17. ALL MANHOLES TO HAVE 3 COATS OF EPOXY PAINT PROTECTION LINING TO ALL EXPOSED INTERNAL CONCRETE SURFACES. 18. INTERNAL CEMENT MORTAR JOINTS OF STORM MANHOLE EXTENSION RINGS SHALL BE RAKED OUT AND ALL EXPOSED FACES SHALL BE LAMINATED WITH EPOXY PAINT. 19. ALL PIPES CONNECTED TO THE MANHOLES ARE TO BE PROVIDED WITH ADEQUATE PUDDLE FLANGES AS REQUIRED. 20. ALL STORM MANHOLES SHALL BE FITTED WITH HEAVY DUTY D400 DI COVERS TO BS EN 124. 21. GRANULAR BED AND SURROUND TO PIPES SHALL BE ENCLOSED IN GEOTEXTILE AS SPECIFIED FOR ALL PIPES. 22. ANY PIPELINE BELOW GROUND LEVEL ENTERING OR PROTRUDING FROM ANY STRUCTURE SHALL BE FITTED WITH TWO FLEXIBLE JOINTS ADJACENT TO THE STRUCTURE AS SPECIFIED UNLESS INDICATED OTHERWISE. 23. CONCRETE SURROUND SHALL BE PROVIDED TO STORMWATER PIPES WHERE THE COVER IS LESS THAN 1.2 METERS. 24. THE OIL INTERCEPTORS SHOWN IN THE DRAWINGS ARE OPTIONAL AND WILL BE USED IN CASE THERE IS NO OIL INTERCEPTOR LOCATED BEFORE THE POND IN THE WADI AREA. 25. INLET TYPE (EITHER CATCH BASIN OR KERB INLET) ARE INDICATIVE FOLLOWING THE DESIGN AND CORRIDORS. IN CASE CONTRACTOR FOUND ON SITE THAT TYPE OF INLET NEEDS TO BE CHANGED FOLLOWING THE ROAD AND SITE CONDITIONS , HE CAN PROCEED ACCORDINGLY. 26. HOUSE CONNECTIONS LOCATIONS ARE INDICATIVE AND TO BE CONFIRMED WITH PLOT OWNERS. 27. HOUSE CONNECTIONS OF PUMPSTATIONS TO BE CONNECTED TO THE OUTLET PIPES COMING FROM THE PUMP STATIONS

excerpt: Overview Th document describes the Utility Identification Survey scope of works to be conducted in DII (Area shown in schematic below). The infrastructure package is divided in 3 packages: Package I, Package II and Package III. The below scope of works covers Package I currently but will extend to Packages II and III as optional after agreement with the Client. The information for existing networks for dry and wet utilities has been obtained from the stakeholders/ service providers; however, the accuracy of the information needs to be validated to avoid unforeseen circumstances/ scenarios. This is also fundamental as utility service provisions to existing users will need to be maintained till specific and discrete dates. The existing service connections will be terminated in phases, as the areas become available. The survey should give DGCL a comprehensive picture on the existing utility infrastructure in the highlighted area(s) above which will allow them to identify and quantify to the highest degree of accuracy the amount of utility protection, demolition, diversion needed to carry out the proposed Master Plan in the said zone. Existing Information The available information for the existing utilities with the Client is included herewith and covers the below. It is to be noted that all the information provided as part of the scope of works is to be treated as ‘For Information Only’. Any text/notes on the drawing not relevant will be ignored. HV Network (Appendix ‘A’) MV Network (Appendix ‘B’) LV Network (Appendix ‘C’) Telecom Network including GCC Cable (Appendix ‘D’) Potable Water Network (Appendix ‘E’) Wastewater Network (Appendix ‘F’) In addition to the above, topographical survey of the area is also available, as ‘For Information Only’, which can be made available to the Contractor upon request. Scope To provide a Complete Utility Identification Survey Report for DII Project Site, based on the following list of minimum works but not limited to: Supervision of the works. The Contractor must ensure to liaise with the Construction Supervision supervising its works to ensure that all procedures are stablished in advance of starting the works. Site Visits. Coordinate and conduct a comprehensive site visit for understanding the client’s requests and needs. The Contractor will ensure full compliance with Safety standards as per Contract. As-Built records/drawings. Before starting works on site, the contractor will endeavour all efforts to secure as much information (as-built records and drawings/ any other relevant information) as possible about all relevant buried and above ground assets to be surveyed, by establishing contact with Authorities and Service Providers and report on its findings accordingly. Pre-condition photographic survey. Before starting any works that includes physically impacting existing assets or the ground (excavation, opening of existing structures, excavation of trial trenches, etc), The contractor will ensure to collect extensive photographical evidence of all the surrounding pre-existing conditions of the assets. The originals of the survey report and the photographs and negatives shall be handed over to the Engineer within two (2) weeks of the completion of the survey, one (1) copy retained by the Contractor, and one (1) copy handed over to the Employer at the same time. 7.4 Existing Services The Contractor shall undertake all the necessary requirements to identify any existing services that are/potential to be impacted by the associated works in the Contract. Where works are to be undertaken in areas containing existing services, the Contractor shall establish their precise location by hand-digging trenches or by other suitable means such as electronic scanning before laying any adjacent new service. The Contractor shall provide such information regarding existing services to the Engineer and shall include such details on his record and as-built drawings. The Contractor shall liaise with all service providers to confirm and identify all existing services information. In the event of unknown services being discovered during the carrying out of the Works, the Contractor shall immediately inform the Engineer in writing. Payment for diverting or sealing off and abandoning any of these services if necessary or working around the same will only be made where the proviso to (Information and Inspection) the Conditions of Contract applies and even then, only against certified records and subject to the prior authorization of the Engineer with the consent of the Employer. The Contractor shall locate dimensionally on its as-built drawings all services encountered on the Site. 7.5 Third Party Approvals and Notices The Contractor’s responsibility shall be to carry out and complete the whole of the Works to comply as a minimum with the requirements of each and every relevant statutory, regulatory and utilities authorities. Should the Contractor for any reason whatsoever cause such approvals, permits, consents, etc to be withdrawn, the Contractor shall be fully responsible for their reinstatement or re-issuance, irrespective of whether such were originally procured by the Employer. The Contractor shall not commence any element of the project including but not limited to; demolition, excavation, filling, construction or any other works until he has obtained written approval from the relevant statutory, regulatory and utilities authorities, and a copy of that approval has been submitted to the Engineer. The Contractor’s general obligations shall include, without limitation: a. obtaining the necessary approvals/ permits/ consents, etc for excavation works; b. the submission of the Contactor’s temporary works designs and shop drawings to the relevant authorities and Engineer, obtaining both approvals as applicable; c. complying with the relevant requirements of the Employer’s environmental commitments and any future requirements included within the updated environmental approvals with respect to the construction of the works; 189 of 216

THE CONTRACTOR SHALL VALIDATE THE PUMP HEAD OF THE PUMPS IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE FINAL ARRANGEMENTS OF PIPE, FITTINGS AND NETWORK. 6. CONTRACTOR SHALL DESIGN THE FIRE FIGHTING SYSTEM IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE SAUDI BUILDING CODE. 7. ROCKER PIPES TO BE PROVIDED IMMEDIATELY ADJACENT TO ALL STRUCTURE FACES WHERE BURIED PIPELINE PASSES THROUGH THE STRUCTURE. 8. CONTRACTOR SHALL VERIFY THE MINIMUM SUMP WATER LEVEL IN CONSULTATION WITH THE PUMP MANUFACTURER. 9. A MINIMUM 250MM OR LENGTH OF BOLT SHALL BE MAINTAINED BETWEEN THE FLANGE AND THE WALL. 10. ALL PIPE WORK SHALL BE PN16 RATED UNLESS OTHERWISE SPECIFIED AND SHALL BE INTERNALLY & EXTERNALLY COATED WITH FUSION BONDED EPOXY TO THE APPROVAL OF THE ENGINEER. 11. VENT PIPES WITH NON-RETURN VALVES SHALL BE PROVIDED FOR SCREEN CHAMBER, WET WELL AND VALVE CHAMBERS. 12. DISMANTLING JOINTS ARE PROVIDED FOR FLEXIBILITY AND REMOVAL OF PIPES AND FITTINGS. WHERE FLANGE ADAPTORS PROPOSED, FLANGES SHALL BE SUITABLY TIED WITH THE NEAREST TIE FLANGE ON THE PIPE. THE ADJACENT PIPE SHALL BE PROVIDED WITH TIE FLANGE. 13. TIE IN CONNECTIONS TO OUTSIDE PIPEWORK (TILL 1 METER FROM THE BOUNDARY OF THE PUMPING STATION) SHALL BE OF PUMPING STATION CONTRACTOR'S SCOPE. THE DIAMETER AND MATERIAL SHALL BE CO-ORDINATED ACCURATELY WITH THE NETWORK OUTSIDE. 14. SUPPORT DETAILS FOR ALL EQUIPMENT INCLUDING PUMPS & VESSELS SHALL BE CONFIRMED BY THE CONTRACTOR/MANUFACTURER. 15. ADEQUATE SUPPORTS SHALL BE PROVIDED FOR ALL THE ABOVE GROUND PIPING. 16. THE CONTRACTOR SHALL DEVELOP OUTLINE STRUCTURAL AND ARCHITECTURAL DESIGN AND SUBMIT AS PART OF THEIR TENDER DESIGN. 17. THE CONTRACTOR IS ENTIRELY RESPONSIBLE FOR THE FOLLOWING; A. ARCHITECTURAL DESIGN IN COORDINATION WITH THE CLIENT. B. STRUCTURAL DESIGN AND STRUCTURAL BASIS OF DESIGN CRITERIA. C. SITE DRAINAGE STRATEGY. D. FIRE AND LIFE SAFETY STRATEGY AND DESIGN. E. MECHANICAL AND ELECTRICAL BUILDING SERVICES DESIGN. F. AUTHORITY APPROVALS. G. CONNECTIVITY WITH THE EXTERNAL WET UTILITIES AND DRY UTILITIES NETWORKS. H. CONNECTIVITY WITH THE ROADS. I. SITE GEOTECHNICAL INVESTIGATION AND TOPOGRAPHIC SURVEY. 18. THE CONTRACTOR SHALL INSTALL ALL FUTURE PIPEWORK SUCH AS PIPES WITH PUDDLE FLANGES, SO THAT NO DEMOLITION OF CIVIL WORK IS REQUIRED IN FUTURE. 19. PORTABLE LIFTING DAVIT SHALL BE PROVIDED FOR EACH LIFTING STATION WITH SOCKETS PROPOSED AT ALL LOCATIONS TO LIFT THE PUMPS AND VALVES. 20. ACTIVATED CARBON FILTERS SHALL BE PROVIDED FOR SMALL LIFTING STATIONS. FOR LARGER LIFT STATIONS BIOTRICKLING FILTER WITH ACTIVATED CARBON POLISHING SHALL BE PROVIDED, WHERE THE DESIGN SHALL BE IN CONSULTATION WITH ODOR CONTROL SYSTEM MANUFACTURER. 21. INTERIOR AND EXTERIOR SURFACES OF PUMPING STATION TO BE LINED IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE SPECIFICATION. 22. PUMP STOOL SUPPORT DETAILS TO BE CONFIRMEDBY THE CONTRACTOR TO THE APPROVAL OF THE ENGINEER FOLLOWING PUMP SELECTION. 23.

excerpt: Detailed Design Report Package 1 IP-INF-054-0000-JCB-RPT-DE-000013-A 29 Value Engineering 29.1 General As part of the DGII infrastructure design delivery process, value engineering study is an integral part of the design development process. The VE study process defines a sequence of activities that are undertaken during a VE study; before, during, and following a workshop. During the VE workshop, the VE team learns about the background issues, defines and classifies the project functions, identifies creative approaches to provide the functions, and then evaluates, develops, and presents the VE proposals to key decision makers. The VE methodology consists of seven sequential phases as depicted in Figure 29-1: below. Those are information, function analysis, evaluation, creative, develop recommendations, presentation, and finally implementation and follow-up. Each phase has its own purpose, objectives, and tasks. For example, the creative phase involves exploring the various ways to perform the function(s) identified in the function analysis phase. This allows team members to brainstorm alternatives to existing systems or methods that are in use. Brainstorming forces people to be creative and allows team members to speculate on all possible ideas to the problems presented, or alternatives to the function. Figure 29-1: Proposed Value Engineering Process for DGII Infrastructure Project Jacobs ideal proposition for DGII is to conduct VE workshop soon after completion of 60% preliminary design and cost estimates. Subsequently, the outcome of the VE workshop shall be implemented during the execution of the 60% preliminary design stage. Soon after completion of this stage and cost estimates are adjusted accordingly, a second round of VE workshop was conducted on 6th April 2023 for gauging the previous implementation and identifying plausible areas that could possibly be fine-tuned and implemented during the execution of the 90% preliminary design and for generating new VE ideas. Based on final VE session, VE initiative has been included in the Package 1 detailed design. 29.2 Value Engineering Basics by validating functionality and providing an equal or better solution without compromising the efficacy of the service or product. At present, the Value Methodology Basics followed by Jacobs for DGII VE exercise is as per SAVE International VE process. Value is defined as the ratio of function to cost and thus value can be increased by either improving the function or by reducing the cost. Value = Function / Cost The value engineering should be initiated as early as possible in the project life cycle. If value engineering becomes rework or causes project delays, it is no longer beneficial to the project. The below graph shows when value engineering moves from presenting a financial gain to a financial loss. The lower down the project cycle we implement value engineering, it may become counterproductive to the overall project budget. excerpt: Detailed Design Report_extract Package 1 - IP-INF-054-0000-JCB-RPT-DE-000013 [A] 24 January 2024 Potable Water and Firefighting (page 154 and next) “It shall be noted that the potable water alignment and design was based on the Masterplan of DGII 14.1.5 Rev08, further changes in the masterplan shall be considered in the upcoming submissions.” Introduction The concept of potable water system is to take main supply from National Water Company (NWC) water line 1200 mm (JF: or 1000mm as mention ahead?) located in King Khalid Road (KKR) (under construction) (JF: details of this project? Work programme coordinated with ours?) to supply the three proposed tanks in the development. Connection points: 2 in the north side of the development feeding Tank-1 and Tank-2 and 1 in the south side of KKR feeding Tank-3. The distribution system should include water connection to each building unit up to its boundary plot maintaining minimum pressure requirement as per NWC/MEWA standards. Individual plots developers shall be responsible for the design and construction of their internal potable water distribution systems. (Easting and Northing) shall be confirmed with NWC & DGCL. Design objectives and constraints Main objective of the hydraulic design is to achieve a minimum pressure requirement of 1.5 bar at all locations. The information about existing pressure at the source point in NWC network on the KKR road is not available yet, The design will be amended in the later stage’s once information about pressure at tie-in point and location is confirmed by the authority (JF: this is a major constrain and may lead to time and/or cost impact) Existing Potable Water Network The (existing) network is seen to be located along King Khalid Road (KKR), within Districts DE3, 5, 7, 8, and 11. Pipe diameters are varying in size from 110 mm to 1200 mm. Pipe material for the combined potable water/firefighting systems includes uPVC, Cast Iron (CI), Ductile Iron (DI) and Asbestos Cement (AC), Concrete Cylindrical Pipe (CCP). All existing AC pipes within the project boundary will have to be replaced and adequality removed according to health organizations standards. These include the 300 mm and 600 mm diameter pipelines along King Khalid Road. Discussion and coordination with NWC on these alternatives shall take place. (JF: work by which project? Infra? Demolitions?. Coordination required between AIC and third party/stakeholder) Design Basis and Criteria Three storage reservoirs will be provided with total storage as one-day average demand plus fire water requirement (893 m3 in each tank (31 L/S for 4 Hours at two Hydrants), as a minimum level of redundancy. The pumps design shall follow the Peak daily Demand plus Fire Fighting demand (PDD + FF) and to assure minimum pressure in the network at the plot connection = 1.5 bar and maximum pressure up to 5.0 bar. House connection Type: As per NWC standards, a water connection will be composed of a saddle connection mounted on a waterline, connection pipes, water meter boxes and other related and necessary items to complete the house connection assembly…. size shallaccommodate filling the plot storage tank in 8 hours as per the NFPA

The importance of pipe detecting and the value of its application. Before excavation for maintenance of underground piping, it is necessary to understand the various site problems on topography and surface materials (e.g. position (depth and displacement) and size of other piping, as well as manholes); In order to prevent third party companies from possible damages to infrastructural equipments and people, severe damage will be generated from mistaken excavation of other piping. The severity might even affect the corporate image and living resources such as electricity, telecommunication and hydrology. Detection of underground pipeline and cable locations is very important, in addition, locations and positions of infrastructural elements with respect to each other must be known for the new infrastructural projects and for the process of operation and replacement of current infrastructure. 1.1. Introduction Developing Technologies are rapidly, so there are a lot of devices for the detection of pipeline and cable locations. These devices are working with two methods in general. One of them is electromagnetic detection method with electromagnetic induction, and the other is GPR (Ground Penetrating Radar) method working with the principle of determining the underground structure and underground holes. Especially with the new instruments and computer algorithms developed in the last years, the locations of infrastructural elements with respect to each other are determined more accurately. Ground penetrating radar (GPR) is a geophysical method that uses radar pulses to image the subsurface. This non-destructive method uses electromagnetic (EM) radiation in the microwave band (UHF/VHF frequencies) of the radio spectrum, and detects the reflected signals from subsurface structures. One of the most useful applications of GPR in urban infrastructural engineering is mapping and detection of buried pipes. This unique application becomes imperative due to the ever-growing urbanization in both developed and developing nations with its attendant demand for buried utilities. The construction, development and management of subsurface infrastructures has become a very viable business that attracts the attention of scientists and engineers over the past few years. Various utilities such as telecommunication and electric power cables, water and gas supply cables etc. are delivered through underground pipes of various sized buried at different depths. In many cases, maintenance of these infrastructures requires digging operation which leads to unintentional damage to some of the facilities. Overview This document describes the Utility Identification Survey scope of works to be conducted in DII (Area shown in schematic below). The infrastructure package is divided in 3 packages: Package I, Package II and Package III. The below scope of works covers Package I currently but will extend to Packages II and III as optional after agreement with the Client. The information for existing networks for dry and wet utilities has been obtained from the stakeholders/ service providers; however, the accuracy of the information needs to be validated to avoid unforeseen circumstances/ scenarios. This is also fundamental as utility service provisions to existing users will need to be maintained till specific and discrete dates. The existing service connections will be terminated in phases, as the areas become available. The survey should give DGCL a comprehensive picture on the existing utility infrastructure in the highlighted area(s) above which will allow them to identify and quantify to the highest degree of accuracy the amount of utility protection, demolition, diversion needed to carry out the proposed Master Plan in the said zone. DII UTILITY IDENTIFICATION SURVEY – Scope of Works AECOM Page 3 of 19 Information Classification: Public 2. Existing Information The available information for the existing utilities with the Client is included herewith and covers the below. It is to be noted that all the information provided as part of the scope of works is to be treated as ‘For Information Only’. Any text/notes on the drawing not relevant will be ignored. • HV Network (Appendix ‘A’) • MV Network (Appendix ‘B’) • LV Network (Appendix ‘C’) • Telecom Network including GCC Cable (Appendix ‘D’) • Potable Water Network (Appendix ‘E’) • Wastewater Network (Appendix ‘F’) In addition to the above, topographical survey of the area is also available, as ‘For Information Only’, which can be made available to the Contractor upon request. 3. Scope To provide a Complete Utility Identification Survey Report for DII Project Site, based on the following list of minimum works but not limited to: 1- Supervision of the works. The Contractor must ensure to liaise with the Construction Supervision supervising its works to ensure that all procedures are stablished in advance of starting the works. 2- Site Visits. Coordinate and conduct a comprehensive site visit for understanding the client’s requests and needs. The Contractor will ensure full compliance with Safety standards as per Contract. 3- As-Built records/drawings. excerpt: # Design Review and Acceptance Procedure ## Scope The design review and acceptance procedure governs the review and acceptance of design documents within the construction programme. It applies to all design submissions from consultants, architects, and engineers. ## Valid Design Review Statuses Only these statuses are permitted on design documents under the design review procedure:ign documents under the design review procedure: - `FOR_COMMENT` — issued for review and feedback - `ACCEPTANCE` — accepted for use without further comment - `BUY_OFF` — closed-out / agreed; no further iteration required - `PENDING_DEBRIEF` — awaiting formal debrief meeting - `SUPERSEDED` — replaced by a newer revision Plain-language equivalents permitted on the title block: `accepted`, `for comment`, `buy-off`. ## Forbidden Statuses on Design Documentsoff`. ## Forbidden Statuses on Design Documents These statuses are contractually prohibited on design documents and must never appear on design submissions: - `APPROVED` - `APPROVAL` - `SIGN_OFF` ### Why APPROVED Is Forbidden The word `APPROVED` carries contractual liability. It implies that the reviewer has accepted the design and assumes responsibility for its content. The design review procedure explicitly prohibits this word on design documents to preserve the contractor's liability for design correctness. Use `accepted`, `for comment`, or `buy-off` instead. ### What This Means In Practice - A QA officer who stamps a structural drawing `APPROVED` is non-compliant with the design review procedure. The drawing must be re-stamped with one of the valid statuses. - A Lead Engineer cath one of the valid statuses. - A Lead Engineer cannot use `APPROVED` regardless of seniority — the prohibition applies to all signatories. - The same rule applies to `APPROVAL` and `SIGN_OFF`. ## Review Distribution Period ### Minimum Distribution Period Design review packages must be distributed to relevant stakeholders at least **7 calendar days** before the scheduled Design Review Workshop. This is a minimum — anything shorter is non-compliant.s a minimum — anything shorter is non-compliant. The 7-day figure is **calendar days**, not business days. Weekends and public holidays count toward the period. ### Maximum Distribution Period The design review procedure recommends a maximum distribution period of 14 calendar days. Distributing too far in advance encourages stakeholders to defer review and can dilute attention. ### Common Misconceptioncan dilute attention. ### Common Misconception The minimum review period is **not 30 days**. Some teams cite 30 days from other procedures or contract clauses; the design review procedure is explicit on 7 calendar days minimum. ### Worked Example If the Design Review Workshop is scheduled for the 15th of the month, the review pack must be issued no later than the 8th of that month. Distributing on the 8th gives exactly 7 calendar days before the 15th.h gives exactly 7 calendar days before the 15th. If the pack is distributed only 3 calendar days before the workshop, the workshop must be postponed by at least 4 additional calendar days to comply. ## Related Procedures - Design directive procedure — Design Directives and Employer Approval - Change management procedure — Variation Orders vs Request for Modification (RFM) - Non-conformance procedure — Non-Conformance Reports (NCR)

excerpt: # Interior Finishes Take-off and Estimate — the Process Contract How interior quantities and resource costs are derived on this platform. This document states the PROCESS. It deliberately contains **no heights, no productivity figures, no rates**: those are project variables that change per project and even per floor, and they must come from the project's own documents, the project facts store, or the operator — never from a global default. ## The processr — never from a global default. ## The process 1. **Measure** — the drawing take-off gives, per floor: net room floor area, summed room perimeter, and room count (`drawing_qto`). 2. **Derive interior quantities** — `interior_finishes_takeoff` computes: - floor screed / floor tiling / ceiling finish areas = net floor area; - skirting length = perimeter − (doors × door width); - wall finish area = perimeter × floor-to-ceiling height − door area − window deductions;ling height − door area − window deductions; - blockwork element area = wall face area × shared-wall fraction (internal walls are shared between two rooms; the fraction is a declared modelling parameter). The calculator REFUSES when the height is missing — it names the variable to supply instead of assuming one. 3. **Split resources** — `resource_line_cost` computes, per line: labour = quantity ÷ daily output × trade day rate; plant = declared÷ daily output × trade day rate; plant = declared fraction of labour; material = quantity × material rate. Productivity and day rate are required inputs; a missing material rate is reported as NO SOURCED RATE, never as zero and never invented. 4. **Source the variables, per project** — in this order: - the project's own documents (sections and door schedules for heights and openings; priced bills for rates);ights and openings; priced bills for rates); - the project facts / memory store (values the operator confirmed for THIS project — heights per floor, agreed norms, market rates); - the curated knowledge base's published references (composite rates, trade day rates, material prices) — cited by source; - the operator, asked directly, when none of the above carries the value. 5. **Declare** — every deliverable restates the variables used and theirdeliverable restates the variables used and their source. An estimate whose basis section cannot name where each variable came from is not finished. ## Why no defaults A default height or norm silently wrong for one floor poisons every quantity derived from it, and the error is invisible because nothing asked for the value. A refusal that names the missing variable costs one question; a wrong hardwired fact costs a re-measure. The calculators therefore fail loudly on missing required variables, and agents ask.

excerpt: # Design Objectives — The 8+1 Whole-Building Goals (WBDG) Reference guidance on the design objectives a high-performance building must balance. Source: WBDG Design Objectives. Best-practice guidance (how to think about a design), not a regulation or binding standard — the project brief and the client's requirements govern priorities. International practice, applies to KSA. These objectives are interdependent: a good design integrates them rather than optimising one in isolation. Grounds how the platform reasons about design trade-offs and brief/BOD analysis. ## The design objectives## The design objectives | Objective | What it means | |---|---| | Accessible | Usable by people of all abilities; accessible routes, entrances, and facilities (universal design). | | Aesthetics | The form, materials, and image of the building and its fit with context. | | Cost-Effective | Best value over the whole life cycle — life-cycle cost, not lowest first cost; value engineering. | | Functional / Operational | Meets the functional programme; systems integration, flexibility, durability, operability. | | Historic Preservation | Respects historic/existing fabric; adaptive reuse where relevant. | | Productive | Occupant comfort, health, and productivity — thermal comfort, lighting, acoustics, indoor air quality, ergonomics. | | Resilient | Resists and recovers from hazards and disruptions — robustness, redundancy, adaptability. | | Secure / Safe | Physical security, life safety, fire protection, and natural-hazard mitigation. | | Sustainable | Environmental performance — energy, water, materials, site, and indoor environmental quality (the home of LEED-type goals). |Source: WBDG Design Objectives. ## How they work together - The objectives are **interdependent** — decisions for one affect others (e.g. a sustainability move can improve productivity but change cost). A high-performance design evaluates and balances them, it does not maximise one alone. - **Cost-Effective** is judged on **whole-life cost** (life-cycle cost analysis), not first cost — durability, energy, and maintenance count.cost — durability, energy, and maintenance count. - **Sustainable** is where rating systems (e.g. LEED) live; WBDG frames the goal, the specific rating credits are a separate standard. ## How to use - Use this to explain what each objective covers and that they must be balanced. - The project brief / Owner's Project Requirements set the priority weighting for a specific project — this is the general framework. - When analysing a brief or basis of design, check which objectives are addressed and flag gaps (e.g. resilience or accessibility not mentioned) rather than inventing requirements.

excerpt: # EVM Thresholds and Traffic Light System ## CPI and SPI — Definitions **CPI (Cost Performance Index)** = EV ÷ AC - CPI > 1.0 means cost efficient — earned value exceeds actual cost. - CPI = 1.0 means on budget. - CPI < 1.0 means over budget — earned value is less than actual cost. **SPI (Schedule Performance Index)** = EV ÷ PV (also expressed as BCWP ÷ BCWS) - SPI > 1.0 means ahead of schedule. - SPI = 1.0 means on schedule. - SPI < 1.0 means behind schedule.on schedule. - SPI < 1.0 means behind schedule. Interpretation note: an SPI of 0.8 means the project has earned only 80 cents of value for every dollar planned. An SPI below 1.0 always means the project is behind schedule. ## CPI Traffic Light System The CPI Traffic Light is the standard executive-dashboard rule: - **GREEN — CPI > 1.00** — Under Budget, Cost Efficient. Keep doing what works. - **AMBER — 0.90 ≤ CPI ≤ 1.00** — Slightly Over Budget. Investigate and take action.lightly Over Budget. Investigate and take action. - **RED — CPI < 0.90** — Over Budget, Cost Inefficient. Take corrective action now. The RED threshold is **CPI < 0.90**. Anything below 0.90 is RED. The AMBER band is **0.90 ≤ CPI ≤ 1.00** (inclusive on both ends). A CPI of exactly 0.90 is AMBER. A CPI of exactly 1.00 is AMBER. The GREEN band is **CPI > 1.00** (strictly greater than 1.00). ### Worked Examplestrictly greater than 1.00). ### Worked Examples - CPI of 0.85 → RED (below the 0.90 threshold). - CPI of 0.91 → AMBER (above 0.90, within the 0.90-1.00 band). - CPI of 0.93 → AMBER. - CPI of 0.95 → AMBER. - CPI of 1.05 → GREEN (above 1.00). - CPI of 0.72 → RED. Action required: forensic cost-variance analysis and a recovery plan. The project is materially overspending against earned value. ## SPI Traffic Light Systemainst earned value. ## SPI Traffic Light System - **GREEN — SPI > 1.00** — Ahead of Schedule. Maintain momentum. - **AMBER — 0.90 ≤ SPI ≤ 1.00** — Slightly Behind. Review plan and recover. - **RED — SPI < 0.90** — Behind Schedule, At Risk. Take corrective action now. ## Combined CPI / SPI Interpretation Both indices together describe project health: - CPI > 1.0 AND SPI > 1.0 → Ahead and under budget. Great performance. - CPI < 1.0 AND SPI > 1.0 → Ahead but over budget. Monitor costs.SPI > 1.0 → Ahead but over budget. Monitor costs. - CPI > 1.0 AND SPI < 1.0 → On budget but behind. Recover schedule. - CPI < 1.0 AND SPI < 1.0 → Behind and over budget. Take corrective action immediately. ## TCPI — To-Complete Performance Index TCPI = (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC) TCPI is the cost efficiency required for the remaining work to complete on budget. excerpt: # Fall Protection — Site Safety Criteria (OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M) REAL, sourced fall-protection thresholds for construction sites. Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.502 (Subpart M), US federal regulation, public domain. This is a US-reference standard: in Saudi Arabia site HSE is governed by Saudi labour law (MHRSD) and the project's approved HSE plan, not OSHA — but Saudi practice broadly aligns with these figures. Use as an engineering reference; enforce against the project HSE plan. Values are metric-led (SI) with the original US-customary figure, as written in the regulation, in parentheses. ## Guardrail systems## Guardrail systems | Parameter | Value (SI) | Original (US) | |---|---|---| | Top-rail height above walking surface | 1.1 m (± 8 cm) | 42 in (± 3 in) | | Top-rail minimum strength (force withstood) | 890 N | 200 lbf | | Maximum opening / midrail gap | 0.48 m | 19 in | | Toeboard minimum vertical height | 9 cm | 3½ in |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.502(b), (j). ## Personal fall arrest system (PFAS)## Personal fall arrest system (PFAS) | Parameter | Value (SI) | Original (US) | |---|---|---| | Maximum arresting force on the body (harness) | 8 kN | 1,800 lbf | | Maximum free-fall distance | 1.8 m | 6 ft | | Maximum deceleration distance | 1.07 m | 3½ ft | | Anchorage strength, per attached worker | 22.2 kN | 5,000 lbf |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.502(d). Note: anchorage may instead be part of a system designed and used under a qualified person's supervision at a safety factor of 2. ## Hole and opening covers Covers over holes must be capable of supporting at least twice the combined weight of workers, equipment, and materials that may be imposed on them (rated to 2x the imposed load), and must be secured and colour-coded or marked "HOLE" / "COVER". Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.502(i). ## KSA applicability: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.502(i). ## KSA applicability OSHA 1926 is US federal site-safety law and is not the governing authority in Saudi Arabia. Site HSE in KSA is regulated under Saudi labour law (MHRSD) and the project's approved HSE/safety plan; SBC (Saudi Building Code) governs building design, not site safety. These thresholds are a US engineering reference. Saudi practice broadly aligns: guardrails ~1.0–1.1 m high, a1.8 m free-fall limit, andails ~1.0–1.1 m high, a1.8 m free-fall limit, and PFAS anchorage in the 22 kN range. Where a value is enforced on site, confirm it against the project HSE plan. ## How to use - Fall protection is generally required at a fall height of 1.8 m (6 ft) or more in construction (Subpart M general trigger, 1926.501). - Quote the SI value for site use; cite the US original and the regulation number so the basis is traceable. - State that this is a US-reference figure and that the project HSE plan / local regulation takes precedence where they differ. - Do not present OSHA as the legal authority for a Saudi project — it is a reference standard

The project is the Middle East's largest integrated leisure and theme park destination located on Sheikh Zayed road in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Spread over 25 million square feet, it features more than 100 rides and attractions, and consists of three theme parks: Motiongate Dubai, Bollywood Parks Dubai and Legoland Dubai, and one water park: Legoland Water Park. lt also encompasses Riverland Dubai, a themed retail and dining destination, as well as the Polynesian-themed family resort, Lapita Hotel. Chadi was assigned to my package The Riverland even though he is coming from EPC Oil and Gas environment he demonstrated great skills as Client Representative PMC managing various main contractors and consultants adopting a fast track multi-package strategy. Chadi is highly recommended for his technical expertise, he made the right decisions for day to day activities to meet the challenge and deliver the project on time with zero delay. ALJAZZAR g) ip ot I MOHAMMED OMAR JAZZAR CONSULTING ENGINEERS CO Auwsigl GILaiuS Ne ae dane AS yc 1. Statement of Problem Urban infrastructures are becoming more complex last century. The importance of pipe detecting and the value of its application. Before excavation for maintenance of underground piping, it is necessary to understand the various site problems on topography and surface materials (e.g. position (depth and displacement) and size of other piping, as well as manholes); In order to prevent third party companies from possible damages to infrastructural equipments and people, severe damage will be generated from mistaken excavation of other piping. The severity might even affect the corporate image and living resources such as electricity, telecommunication and hydrology. Detection of underground pipeline and cable locations is very important, in addition, locations and positions of infrastructural elements with respect to each other must be known for the new infrastructural projects and for the process of operation and replacement of current infrastructure. 1.1. Introduction Developing Technologies are rapidly, so there are a lot of devices for the detection of pipeline and cable locations. These devices are working with two methods in general. One of them is electromagnetic detection method with electromagnetic induction, and the other is GPR (Ground Penetrating Radar) method working with the principle of determining the underground structure and underground holes. Especially with the new instruments and computer algorithms developed in the last years, the locations of infrastructural elements with respect to each other are determined more accurately. Ground penetrating radar (GPR) is a geophysical method that uses radar pulses to image the subsurface. This non-destructive method uses electromagnetic (EM) radiation in the microwave band (UHF/VHF frequencies) of the radio spectrum, and detects the reflected signals from subsurface structures. One of the most useful applications of GPR in urban infrastructural engineering is mapping and detection of buried pipes. This unique application becomes imperative due to the ever-growing urbanization in both developed and developing nations with its attendant demand for buried utilities. The construction, development and management of subsurface infrastructures has become a very viable business that attracts the attention of scientists and engineers over the past few years. Various utilities such as telecommunication and electric power cables, water and gas supply cables etc. are delivered through underground pipes of various sized buried at different depths. excerpt: Request for Proposals Large-Scale AI Data Center Campus Development Partnership — Canada April 16, 2026 Introduction Anthropic invites qualified parties to submit proposals for the development of a large-scale AI data center campus in Canada. We are seeking partners with the geographic, political, financial, and subject-matter expertise to deliver a collective 1 GW of critical IT capacity (approximately 1.4 GW total utility load) within Canada by EOY 2028, with initial capacity operational by EOY 2027 and a preference for projects that scale further or deliver faster. This is an initial target that may increase, and we will consider a portfolio of smaller sites across several selected respondents where that optimizes for speed. The objective is to establish a secure campus in Canada that supports advanced AI workloads, contributes to Canadian economic development, adds net-new generation capacity and grid infrastructure, and advances Anthropic's mission. Consistent with Anthropic's published energy affordability commitments in the US, we intend to match our load with net-new generation, fund required grid upgrades, and avoid upward pressure on local electricity prices. A performance specification covering data center technical requirements is being made available to developers as Exhibit A. Respondents should review and address compatibility with those requirements in their proposals. Please note that our requirements diverge notably from a typical hyperscaler cloud data center: our SLA model is a two-tier mixed availability model enabling creative energy solutions; we demand higher rack densities and direct-liquid closed-loop cooling (with a baseline design requiring no make-up water for mechanical heat rejection); and we place a higher premium on speed-to-scale over efficiency/reliability. Respondents proposing a standard hyperscale reference product without addressing these deltas will be disadvantaged. Anthropic is briefing relevant federal and provincial government bodies on this RFP in advance of issuance, and is engaging directly with transmission system operators and regulated utilities in candidate provinces. Selection Framework Anthropic is selecting a long-term partner. We expect this RFP process may culminate in an award before all details of design and timing are fully defined. What is most important is that our development partners have the flexibility and comfort to operate in ambiguous and rapidly evolving requirements environments. We are prioritizing partners who demonstrate: - Control of a well-developed land bank and demonstrated ability to identify and transact on additional land parcels as required. - Deep expertise operating in Canada, with demonstrated ability to navigate land development, entitlement, and permitting processes in-province. - Expertise partnering with utilities and power developers (traditional and renewable) to deploy large-scale campus solutions. We are targeting a minimum 1.4 GW (total utility) campus. We understand there is limited Canadian precedent at this scale and will calibrate qualification criteria accordingly. - Demonstrated experience across the full data center delivery lifecycle: design, supply chain, construction, commissioning, and operations. - Financial and development capabilities aligned to a 1+ GW critical IT scale project. - Ability to meet our security requirements across development, design, and operations —internally or through an aligned third-party partnership. Statement of Problem Urban infrastructures are becoming more complex last century. The importance of pipe detecting and the value of its application. Before excavation for maintenance of underground piping, it is necessary to understand the various site problems on topography and surface materials (e.g. position (depth and displacement) and size of other piping, as well as manholes); In order to prevent third party companies from possible damages to infrastructural equipments and people, severe damage will be generated from mistaken excavation of other piping. The severity might even affect the corporate image and living resources such as electricity, telecommunication and hydrology. Detection of underground pipeline and cable locations is very important, in addition, locations and positions of infrastructural elements with respect to each other must be known for the new infrastructural projects and for the process of operation and replacement of current infrastructure. 1.1. Introduction Developing Technologies are rapidly, so there are a lot of devices for the detection of pipeline and cable locations. These devices are working with two methods in general. One of them is electromagnetic detection method with electromagnetic induction, and the other is GPR (Ground Penetrating Radar) method working with the principle of determining the underground structure and underground holes. Especially with the new instruments and computer algorithms developed in the last years, the locations of infrastructural elements with respect to each other are determined more accurately. Ground penetrating radar (GPR) is a geophysical method that uses radar pulses to image the subsurface. This non-destructive method uses electromagnetic (EM) radiation in the microwave band (UHF/VHF frequencies) of the radio spectrum, and detects the reflected signals from subsurface structures. One of the most useful applications of GPR in urban infrastructural engineering is mapping and detection of buried pipes. This unique application becomes imperative due to the ever-growing urbanization in both developed and developing nations with its attendant demand for buried utilities. The construction, development and management of subsurface infrastructures has become a very viable business that attracts the attention of scientists and engineers over the past few years. Various utilities such as telecommunication and electric power cables, water and gas supply cables etc. are delivered through underground pipes of various sized buried at different depths. In many cases, maintenance of these infrastructures requires digging operation which leads to unintentional damage to some of the facilities. excerpt: Document history and status Distribution of copies Executive summary The attached details a number of obstacles following the planned clearance of the SEC site by the end of July 2025. The most concern lies in the connection of utilities which has not been factored into the SEC planned clearance pre-dominantly the reservoir overflow tank which cannot be moved and impedes the storm water connection as per below. The NGL (Natural Ground Level) has been built up with unscreened fill which need to removed to a Municipality dump as part of the works together with a number of other obstacles outlined within this report. Introduction The Contractor has been instructed by the Client to carry out the Gateway-1 Infrastructure work. Gateway-1 is located at the northern side of the Northern Ring Road as indicated in the below pictures. The Scope of the work related to the Infra-1 contractor is indicated in the below snip The area was previously occupied by Saudi Electric Company (SEC) as a laydown area for the construction of the HV substations and network. Following the instruction to AICC to carry out the infrastructure work at Gatweway-1, a site visit was carried out to assess the existing conditions of the site and to enable the site handover from SEC to Infra-1. Site Obstacles Several obstacles within the Right-of-Way (ROW) of the infra-1 have been identified as indicated in the below snip. The details of the above-mentioned obstacles are listed in the below table: Site Topography The site topography has been artificially raised by approximately 1 to 4 meters using unconsolidated fill materials and construction debris (refer to the images below). These materials must be excavated and removed to restore the site to its original natural ground level (NGL) before commencing earthwork activities. At present, the exact volume of these materials cannot be accurately determined due to the lack of historical elevation data. However, a preliminary estimate suggests that the volume of unconsolidated material is approximately 30,000 cubic meters. excerpt: # Design Objectives — The 8+1 Whole-Building Goals (WBDG) Reference guidance on the design objectives a high-performance building must balance. Source: WBDG Design Objectives. Best-practice guidance (how to think about a design), not a regulation or binding standard — the project brief and the client's requirements govern priorities. International practice, applies to KSA. These objectives are interdependent: a good design integrates them rather than optimising one in isolation. Grounds how the platform reasons about design trade-offs and brief/BOD analysis. ## The design objectives## The design objectives | Objective | What it means | |---|---| | Accessible | Usable by people of all abilities; accessible routes, entrances, and facilities (universal design). | | Aesthetics | The form, materials, and image of the building and its fit with context. | | Cost-Effective | Best value over the whole life cycle — life-cycle cost, not lowest first cost; value engineering. | | Functional / Operational | Meets the functional programme; systems integration, flexibility, durability, operability. | | Historic Preservation | Respects historic/existing fabric; adaptive reuse where relevant. | | Productive | Occupant comfort, health, and productivity — thermal comfort, lighting, acoustics, indoor air quality, ergonomics. | | Resilient | Resists and recovers from hazards and disruptions — robustness, redundancy, adaptability. | | Secure / Safe | Physical security, life safety, fire protection, and natural-hazard mitigation. | | Sustainable | Environmental performance — energy, water, materials, site, and indoor environmental quality (the home of LEED-type goals). |Source: WBDG Design Objectives. ## How they work together - The objectives are **interdependent** — decisions for one affect others (e.g. a sustainability move can improve productivity but change cost). A high-performance design evaluates and balances them, it does not maximise one alone. - **Cost-Effective** is judged on **whole-life cost** (life-cycle cost analysis), not first cost — durability, energy, and maintenance count.ost — durability, energy, and maintenance count. - **Sustainable** is where rating systems (e.g. LEED) live; WBDG frames the goal, the specific rating credits are a separate standard. ## How to use - Use this to explain what each objective covers and that they must be balanced. - The project brief / Owner's Project Requirements set the priority weighting for a specific project — this is the general framework. - When analysing a brief or basis of design, check which objectives are addressed and flag gaps (e.g. resilience or accessibility not mentioned) rather than inventing requirements.

Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.502 (Subpart M), US federal regulation, public domain. This is a US-reference standard: in Saudi Arabia site HSE is governed by Saudi labour law (MHRSD) and the project's approved HSE plan, not OSHA — but Saudi practice broadly aligns with these figures. Use as an engineering reference; enforce against the project HSE plan. Values are metric-led (SI) with the original US-customary figure, as written in the regulation, in parentheses. ## Guardrail systems## Guardrail systems | Parameter | Value (SI) | Original (US) | |---|---|---| | Top-rail height above walking surface | 1.1 m (± 8 cm) | 42 in (± 3 in) | | Top-rail minimum strength (force withstood) | 890 N | 200 lbf | | Maximum opening / midrail gap | 0.48 m | 19 in | | Toeboard minimum vertical height | 9 cm | 3½ in |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.502(b), (j). ## Personal fall arrest system (PFAS)## Personal fall arrest system (PFAS) | Parameter | Value (SI) | Original (US) | |---|---|---| | Maximum arresting force on the body (harness) | 8 kN | 1,800 lbf | | Maximum free-fall distance | 1.8 m | 6 ft | | Maximum deceleration distance | 1.07 m | 3½ ft | | Anchorage strength, per attached worker | 22.2 kN | 5,000 lbf |Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.502(d). Note: anchorage may instead be part of a system designed and used under a qualified person's supervision at a safety factor of 2. ## Hole and opening covers Covers over holes must be capable of supporting at least twice the combined weight of workers, equipment, and materials that may be imposed on them (rated to 2x the imposed load), and must be secured and colour-coded or marked "HOLE" / "COVER". Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.502(i)."COVER". Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.502(i). ## KSA applicability OSHA 1926 is US federal site-safety law and is not the governing authority in Saudi Arabia. Site HSE in KSA is regulated under Saudi labour law (MHRSD) and the project's approved HSE/safety plan; SBC (Saudi Building Code) governs building design, not site safety. These thresholds are a US engineering reference. Where a value is enforced on site, confirm it against the project HSE plan. ## How to use - Fall protection is generally required at a fall height of 1.8 m (6 ft) or more in construction (Subpart M general trigger, 1926.501). - Quote the SI value for site use; cite the US original and the regulation number so the basis is traceable. - State that this is a US-reference figure and that the project HSE plan / local regulation takes precedence where they differ. - Do not present OSHA as the legal authority for a Saudi project — it is a reference standard
